Merlin's Magic Squares

AlgebraInvariantsLogic
Game: Make the big board look like the small target board. Each button has a few states, shown as numbers and colours that go round and round.
How to play: Press a big button: it changes, and so do some of its neighbours. Click a small square to change the target. Tick Hint to see how many times to press each button.

Geometry
Look for the math

Number the nine buttons 1 to 9, row by row. A board is then a list of nine numbers, and pressing a button adds a fixed list to it, all counted modulo the number of states N. That is linear algebra on a clock with N hours.

The equation

If s says how many times each button is pressed, then target = board + A s (mod N), where column k of the matrix A is what pressing button k adds. In the plane game a corner adds itself, its two neighbours along the edges and the centre; a side adds the three buttons in its line; the centre adds itself and the four sides. Pressing 1 advances buttons 1, 2, 4 and 5, as the original page says, and the test checks all nine columns.

When can it always be solved?

If A is invertible mod N then s = A⁻¹ (target − board) and every board can be solved in exactly one way, which is the Hint. The determinant of the plane matrix is 5, so it is invertible when N is not a multiple of 5: for N = 2, 3 and 4 (the test checked that the map from presses to boards is one-to-one for each, and not for N = 5). On the torus, where a press advances the whole row and column, the determinant is 80 = 16 · 5, so of 2, 3 and 4 only N = 3 works. The test confirms that torus boards with 2 or 4 states are not all reachable, and that the hint solved every board it was tried on: all 19,683 three-state boards, all 512 × 512 pairs of two-state boards and 200,000 random pairs.

Questions from the page

The order of the presses does not matter (the test shuffled 500 random sequences). The matrix of the plane game has the eigenvalue 1 twice, with two independent eigenvectors; the test finds the double root of the characteristic polynomial and two vectors with A v = v, which also hold mod 2, 3 and 4. And the rules can be found by experiment: set the target to zero, ask the hint for each single-button target, and read off the columns. The third geometry, "Don't touch", has rules you can find that way; they turn out to be the well known Lights Out rules (a button and its four neighbours), with determinant −7.

Choose 2 states and tick Hint, then press the buttons the hint shows. Why does the board come out right?
